title: Multimeters and soldering
blurb: Choose and connect a voltmeter, ammeter or ohmmeter correctly, and tell good solder and joints from bad.

T7D01.why: Electric potential is voltage, and a **voltmeter** measures it.
T7D01.trap: A potentiometer is a variable resistor, not a meter.

T7D02.why: Voltage is measured *between* two points, so a voltmeter connects **in parallel** across the component.
T7D02.trap: In series is how current is measured.

T7D03.why: To measure current, the meter must sit in the path so all current flows through it: **in series**.

T7D04.trap: An ohmmeter reads resistance and a voltmeter reads voltage.

T7D05.why: The ohmmeter **applies a small current and measures the resulting voltage**, which gives resistance by Ohm's law.
T7D05.trap: It doesn't use a variable resistor in series or parallel.

T7D06.why: On the resistance setting the meter supplies its own current, so connecting it across a live voltage can **damage it**.
T7D06.trap: The damaging mistake is voltage on the resistance setting, not the reverse.

T7D07.why: A multimeter measures **voltage and resistance** (and current). Signal strength, impedance and reactance need other instruments.

T7D08.why: **Acid-core** solder has corrosive flux meant for plumbing. Electronics need rosin-core.
T7D08.trap: Lead-tin and rosin-core are the normal electronics choices.

T7D09.why: A cold joint never flowed properly, so it looks **rough or lumpy** and dull. A good joint is smooth and shiny.
T7D09.trap: Bright and shiny is the sign of a good joint.

T7D10.why: The meter's small current **charges the capacitor**, so the resistance reading **keeps increasing with time**.
T7D10.trap: A steady short, open or full-scale reading means something else, like a shorted part.

T7D11.why: The ohmmeter supplies its own test current, so make sure the circuit **is not powered**.
T7D11.trap: Operating voltage, ground and frequency don't matter. Power just adds error.
